name: gltfpack (meshoptimizer)
what: Makes glTF/GLB models smaller and faster to load: builds simplified LODs and compresses meshes and textures for the game build.

simplify.what: Make a lower-poly LOD that keeps a share of the triangles.

aggressive.what: hit the target ratio even if quality suffers

lock_border.what: lock border vertices so connected meshes don't gap

compress.what: Compress the mesh data (EXT_meshopt_compression), optionally turning textures into KTX2/BasisU.

ktx2.what: also convert textures to KTX2 with BasisU

notes: Output needs a loader that supports EXT_meshopt_compression (Godot 4 does not read it out of the box, so test the import; leave compress off for Godot and use simplify only). The README says texture compression (-tc/-tw) only works in the native binaries, not the npm build, which is why this uses release. The macOS zip is built on a macos-15 (arm64) runner. 'gltfpack -v' with no other args prints the version and exits 0; '-h' exits 1. npm alternative: package 'gltfpack', version 1.3.0 in gltf/package.json (registry not reachable from here).

name: AutoRemesher
what: Turns a dense sculpt or scan into clean all-quad topology at a target quad count.

target_quads.what: target quad count (the tool's own default is 50000)

sharp_edge.what: dihedral angle (degrees) treated as a sharp edge

adaptivity.what: how much quads get denser where curvature is high

notes: Headless mode starts when --input is given, but main() still builds a QApplication and MainWindow (it just doesn't show it), so it needs a desktop session. It is built on macos-latest (arm64) and only ad-hoc signed, so Gatekeeper/quarantine has to be cleared. Windows exe is autoremesher.exe inside the zip. name: QuadWild (Bi-MDF)
what: Research-grade quad remesher that follows sharp features and edge flow. Two steps: prepare/trace, then quadrangulate.

prepare.what: Step 1: remesh, compute the field and trace patches; writes <stem>_rem_p0.obj and other files next to the input.

input.what: the mesh (copy it into the workspace first: outputs land next to it)

preset.what: Mechanical keeps sharp edges; Organic for smooth shapes

quadrangulate.what: Step 2: turn the traced patches into a quad mesh; writes <stem>_rem_p0_1_quadrangulation_smooth.obj next to the input.

flow.what: flow.txt tries for better edge flow; flow_noalign.txt is the fallback

notes: There is no -o flag: both binaries write into the input mesh's folder, with names built from the input filename, so LOKI must copy the input into the workspace and then collect the results. Always pass the step argument: the source reads argv[2] even when argc==2. The paths assume the zip is extracted flat into {tool}/ (the zip holds quadwild[.exe], quad_from_patches[.exe], config/, README_release.md). On Windows the second binary is quad_from_patches.exe. The macOS binaries are universal (x86_64 + arm64), unsigned, and need quarantine cleared. There is no zero-exit check command (no args returns 1), so check is null. GPL-3.0 is fine to run as a separate process from AGPL LOKI.

name: Instant Meshes
what: Fast field-aligned retopology to a target face count; quick quad or tri remesh of scans and sculpts.
license: BSD-3-Clause (with an extra clause licensing contributed enhancements back to the authors)

install.manual: There are no GitHub releases (the repo has no tags). Download the prebuilt zip for your OS from the README links: Windows https://instant-meshes.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/Release/instant-meshes-windows.zip, macOS https://instant-meshes.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/instant-meshes-macos.zip, Linux https://instant-meshes.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/instant-meshes-linux.zip. Extract it into <data>/tools/instant-meshes/ and point LOKI's {exe} at 'Instant Meshes.exe' (Windows) or the binary inside 'Instant Meshes.app/Contents/MacOS/' (macOS). The binaries are Intel 64-bit only, so the Mac mini runs them under Rosetta 2. Alternative: build from source with 'git clone --recursive' + 'cmake .' + 'make'.

remesh.what: Batch-remesh to about N faces (pure quads by default).

dominant.what: allow a quad-dominant (mixed) mesh instead of pure quads

notes: Batch mode starts when -o is given with exactly one input and exits 0 on success, without touching the GUI. -h prints help but returns -1, so check is null. -d makes it deterministic (slower but repeatable). Other real flags: -r/--rosy 2|4|6, -p/--posy 4|6, -s/--scale, -v/--vertices (use only one of -s/-f/-v), -c/--crease <deg>, -S/--smooth <iter>, -t/--threads, -i/--intrinsic. On Linux the GUI needs zenity, but batch mode should not. I could not check the S3 zips: the host is blocked from this sandbox, so the exe names inside them are taken from the README text.

name: UniRig auto-rig
what: Predicts a skeleton and skin weights for any character or creature mesh, then merges them into a rigged GLB.

install.manual: Clone UniRig at the ref into {src} and make a Python 3.11 venv (bpy==4.2 needs 3.11). In order: pip install a CUDA build of torch + torchvision; pip install -r requirements.txt; pip install the spconv-cuXXX wheel that matches your CUDA; pip install torch_scatter torch_cluster -f https://data.pyg.org/whl/torch-<torch-version>+<cuda>.html --no-cache-dir; pip install numpy==1.26.4 (all from README 'Installation'). requirements.txt lists flash_attn, which has no official Windows wheel: get a prebuilt wheel that matches your torch/CUDA/Python, or build it (slow, needs the CUDA toolkit + MSVC). The weights download themselves on first run through hf_hub_download(repo_id='VAST-AI/UniRig'). This is manual because the torch/spconv/pyg/flash_attn versions have to match each other and the download indexes could not be reached from here to pin them.

check: import bpy, torch, spconv.pytorch, torch_scatter, torch_cluster, flash_attn; print(torch.cuda.is_available())

rig.what: Full auto-rig: extract, then skeleton, then skin, then merge onto the original mesh, giving a rigged GLB.

seed.what: change for a different skeleton variation

skeleton.what: Skeleton only (FBX), so you can fix bones in Blender/Maya before skinning.

notes: The wrappers replay launch/inference/generate_skeleton.sh, generate_skin.sh, extract.sh and merge.sh with the same module calls and arguments, but without bash (Windows has no bash). They run with cwd={src} because the configs and 'python -m src...' are relative paths. Paths must be absolute, and intermediate npz files go to {src}/tmp, so only run one job at a time. extract.sh also runs 'pip install psutil' at run time, so add psutil to the venv. The task configs use precision bf16-mixed and accelerator gpu, and the skin model imports flash_attn plus spconv/torch_scatter (CUDA only), so it can't run on the Mac mini (no CUDA). VRAM: the repo states no figure, and 8 GB on the 3070 Ti is unconfirmed (the skeleton model is a ~350M-parameter autoregressive transformer and the mesh is decimated to 50k faces). The README says skinning quality drops if the skeleton is wrong; use 'skeleton', fix the bones, then rig. The upstream README points to SkinTokens as the newer successor.

name: MV-Adapter texture generation
what: Paints a full texture onto an untextured mesh from a text prompt or a reference image (multi-view diffusion, then baked to UV).

weights.name: huanngzh/mv-adapter (mvadapter_tg2mv_sd21/_sdxl, mvadapter_ig2mv_sd21/_sdxl .safetensors) + base SD2.1-base or SDXL-base + RealESRGAN_x2plus + big-lama

install.manual: The texture pipeline needs Linux plus CUDA: requirements.txt pulls cvcuda_cu12 (CV-CUDA, which ships Linux wheels only) and nvdiffrast built from git, and mvadapter/utils/mesh_utils/blend.py JIT-compiles a CUDA extension (needs nvcc). On the owner's Windows PC, run it inside WSL2 Ubuntu with the CUDA toolkit. Steps (README 'Installation'): clone at the ref into {src}; pip install torch torchvision from the matching CUDA index; pip install -r requirements.txt; put the two checkpoints into {src}/checkpoints/. The adapter and base-model weights download from Hugging Face on first run.

text_to_texture.what: Texture a mesh from a text prompt; writes <save_dir>/<name>_shaded.glb.

prompt.what: what the object should look like

variant.what: sd21 is the low-VRAM (<10 GB) model; sdxl looks better but needs more

image_to_texture.what: Texture a mesh to match a reference image; writes <save_dir>/<name>_shaded.glb.

remove_bg.what: cut the background out of the reference (downloads BiRefNet)

notes: The wrapper chdirs into {src} because the scripts load ./checkpoints/... by relative path and use relative imports inside the scripts package, so pass absolute paths. VRAM: the README says the SD2.1 geometry adapters need under 10 GB and image-to-multiview at SDXL needs about 14 GB, so on the 8 GB 3070 Ti even sd21 is borderline and sdxl will not fit. Base models used: stabilityai/stable-diffusion-2-1-base (sd21) and stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0 + madebyollin/sdxl-vae-fp16-fix (sdxl); BiRefNet (ZhengPeng7/BiRefNet) for --remove_bg. name: Kimodo text-to-motion (SOMA)
what: Generates human mocap-quality animation from a text prompt (for example 'a person walks forward then waves') and exports BVH for retargeting.

weights.name: nvidia/Kimodo-SOMA-RP-v1.2 (model key kimodo-soma-rp) + text encoder McGill-NLP/LLM2Vec-Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-mntp(-supervised) on gated meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct
weights.license: Kimodo SOMA: NVIDIA Open Model License; text encoder base: Meta Llama 3 Community License (gated)

check: import kimodo, soma; from kimodo.scripts import generate

text_to_motion.what: Text prompt to SOMA-skeleton motion: writes <output>.bvh plus a .npz next to it.

prompt.what: describe the motion; several prompts can be chained as the CLI docs describe

tpose.what: rest pose is a standard T-pose (easier to retarget in Maya/Godot)

notes: SOMA only: the model is hard-wired to kimodo-soma-rp (resolves to nvidia/Kimodo-SOMA-RP-v1.2). Never use kimodo-smplx-rp: its weights are under the NVIDIA R&D (non-commercial) licence and it needs SMPL-X files. The text encoder stays on CPU through TEXT_ENCODER_DEVICE=cpu, which the README says cuts VRAM from ~17 GB to under 3 GB. TEXT_ENCODER_MODE=local skips probing the kimodo_textencoder service on 127.0.0.1:9550. Cost: Llama-3-8B in bfloat16 on CPU needs about 16 GB of system RAM (plan on 32 GB on the PC) and is slow for each run. For batches, run 'kimodo_textencoder' once in the background and drop TEXT_ENCODER_MODE. Mac mini: generate.py only picks cuda or cpu (no MPS) and 16 GB of RAM can't hold the encoder, so darwin is left out. Before the first run, the owner must request access to meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct on Hugging Face and run 'hf auth login' (LOKI cannot do this step for them). pip install builds the bundled MotionCorrection C++ extension, so CMake and a C++ compiler (MSVC or MinGW) must be on PATH. Output: --output X.bvh writes X.bvh (SOMA 77-joint BVH) and X.bvh.npz (Kimodo NPZ: posed_joints, global/local rot mats, foot_contacts, ...). FBX is not offered. SOMA-X (py-soma-x 0.3.4) is installed as the 'soma' extra for skinned viz; BVH export itself doesn't need it. torch==2.6.0 from the cu124 index is a choice LOKI makes, not a pin from the repo (the docs only say PyTorch 2.0+), and the index could not be reached from here.

name: FreeMoCap
what: Multi-camera markerless motion capture (record, calibrate, reconstruct 3D skeletons) with its own app.

install.manual: There is no headless CLI. The 'freemocap' console script (freemocap.__main__:run_main) starts a FastAPI/uvicorn server on localhost:8005 for the Electron/React GUI. name: MediaPipe Pose Landmarker
what: Pulls 33 body landmarks per frame from a single video, for rough reference mocap or animation blocking.
check: import mediapipe as mp, cv2; mp.tasks.vision.PoseLandmarker

video_to_landmarks.what: Run pose landmarking on every frame and write JSON with image-space and world-space (metres, hip-centred) landmarks.
cmd: import sys,json,cv2,mediapipe as mp;V=mp.tasks.vision;L=V.PoseLandmarker.create_from_options(V.PoseLandmarkerOptions(base_options=mp.tasks.BaseOptions(model_asset_path=sys.argv[2]),running_mode=V.RunningMode.VIDEO));c=cv2.VideoCapture(sys.argv[1]);fps=c.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FPS) or 30.0;R=[(int(i*1000/fps),L.detect_for_video(mp.Image(image_format=mp.ImageFormat.SRGB,data=cv2.cvtColor(f,cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)),int(i*1000/fps))) for i,(ok,f) in enumerate(iter(c.read,(False,None)))];L.close();json.dump({'fps':fps,'frames':[{'t_ms':t,'image':[[p.x,p.y,p.z,p.visibility] for p in r.pose_landmarks[0]] if r.pose_landmarks else [],'world':[[p.x,p.y,p.z,p.visibility] for p in r.pose_world_landmarks[0]] if r.pose_world_landmarks else []} for t,r in R]},open(sys.argv[3],'w'))

notes: Only the first detected pose is kept (num_poses defaults to 1). Landmark order is MediaPipe's 33-point BlazePose topology, so it is not a rig and needs retargeting/IK before it can drive a character. opencv-contrib-python comes in as a mediapipe dependency (requirements.txt), which is what supplies cv2. The loop stops when cv2.VideoCapture.read() returns (False, None). Every frame's result is kept in memory, which is fine for clips but not hour-long videos. The lite model URL is the only one found in the repo (mediapipe/tasks/web/vision/README.md). The full/heavy variants probably follow the same pattern but were not checked, and storage.googleapis.com was blocked from here, so the size is approximate. mediapipe 1.1.1 was released 2026-10-14 (PyPI mirror): new and fine, but this is the 1.x ctypes rewrite, so do not mix it with old 0.10 'mp.solutions.pose' code.

name: ufbx
what: Single-file C library that loads FBX/OBJ robustly. Useful inside LOKI or a converter, but not a tool you can run.

install.manual: There is no Python binding and no CLI in the repo: just ufbx.c and ufbx.h, plus bindgen/ (Python scripts that generate a binding IR, not a binding), examples/viewer and examples/picort (a path tracer demo). To use it, compile a small C converter (for example FBX to glTF/OBJ) against ufbx.c, or use a third-party binding. None were checked here.

notes: Licence is friendly (MIT/public domain). For FBX conversion in the shelf today, UniRig's bpy-based pipeline or Blender/Godot importers are the practical routes.
